doc.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: Working with Lou Donaldson, and meeting Mingus
summary: Donaldson hires him and mentors him on tone and time-keeping; he also works briefly with Mingus.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Yeah. That was the start of how I became so cynical. But I met Lou Donaldson the same way. He just came up to me and asked me to work with him. And he had a steady engagement at a small place in the South Bronx, and he was using an organ. It was an organ trio format. And he asked me to work with him. And I said well look if you’re asking me I’m not about to say no to Donaldson. And I did and I became like a son to him. He didn’t have any sons, he just had two daughters. And I was brash and I loved him and he took a liking to me and he championed me and taught me a lot.

I can remember being on the road with him and he’d come to my room in the morning while I was still sleeping, and he’d come in, “Well what did you do last night Jimmy Wormworth?” and blah, blah, blah. And we’d talk and he’d stand in front of me, he’d go to the dresser in my room and stand in front of the mirror and look at his embouchure. Just feel it and press it and examine it and look at it. And one of his idols was Johnny Hodges at the time, curiously enough. Charlie Parker was his main idol, but he loved

Johnny Hodges, I think for his tone. And tone was such a big thing to Lou. And he has such a great tone. And he used to be I think even bigger back then, but he worked on it so much. And he practiced long tones. He was — he taught me a lot. He tried to encourage me to concentrate more on playing the time, just playing the beat on the cymbal, and less on embellishing — comping as it’s called — with my left hand on the snare drum, commenting, filling in. “I’m going to tie your left hand behind your back.” I’d be playing along [scats] finally I’d get tired [scats} and he’d say ‘aah.” It took me a long time before I realized that what he was trying to teach me was that — look, you have to crawl before you can walk and walk before you can run. And you are very talented and you know a lot about music but I’d like to see you concentrate more on just playing the rhythm, keeping the time. Because you know already, you listen and you know when you make good comments, good embellishments with your left hand and with the bass drum, that’s all fine. But you’re only twenty, twenty-one years old and you still can learn how to broaden your effect — broaden what you do. Play the time. Learn how to play the time even better. And it took me a long time before I realized that but I wasn’t about to argue with him. I just felt fortunate and grateful that somebody that was an idol of mine, artistically speaking would want me to be associated with him artistically. And he stood up for me quite a bit. And through him I met Peck Morrison, the bassist, who was Lou’s bassist, man at the time, and we became close. And well I had already met Horace Parlan but we worked together with Lou Donaldson and really became close. And he recommended — well he didn’t recommend me to Mingus, but we worked together with Charlie Mingus for a short time. Charlie Mingus used to come in the Five Spot too when I was working there with Mal Waldron as the house rhythm section. And one time he just asked me to work with him. His regular drummer, his favorite drummer was the late Danny Richmond, but they seemed to have a love-hate relationship. Every two weeks or so Mingus would fire Danny and hire somebody else. And then they’d make up after another two or three days so he’d fire whoever was in effect the sub. And Danny would be back. And that went on.
Mingus pretty much taught Danny Richmond how to play didn’t he?
Danny was a saxophonist, a tenor saxophonist. He was from Lou Donaldson’s home town, Greensboro, North Carolina. I don’t know about that.
It seems like I’d read that somewhere but it may not be true.
I think Danny had started playing the drums before he came to New York. I never heard Danny play the saxophone.
